newsitem.title: KENYA: Rights group accuses Zaire army of gross abuses.
newsitem.headline: Rights group accuses Zaire army of gross abuses.

text.p: Amnesty International on Thursday accused Zairean soldiers retreating from the civil war in eastern Zaire of gross abuses of human rights, raping and killing civilians with impunity.
"People in towns and villages live in constant fear that they will become the next victims of such human rights violations," the London-based human rights group said.

Fears have escalated in the past month since the army launched a counter-offensive to recapture territory lost in the east of the country to rebels since October, Amnesty International said in a report.
Rebels from the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo/Zaire (ADFL) have seized control of a swath of territory around 1,000 km (650 miles) long.
The rebels led by Laurent Kabila say they are liberating Zaire from President Mobutu Sese Seko and the tyranny of an army notorious for indiscipline.

Amnesty said governments appeared unwilling or unable to prevent people suffering at the hands of the army, arguing Zaire slipped from the international agenda after a mass return of Rwandan Hutus from Zaire last November.
Women, members of religious orders and non-Zaireans were targetted by the Zairean Armed Forces (FAZ), the report said.
FAZ troops raped girls at the Lycee Likovi secondary school in Bunia last December 5 or 6, leaving seven girls dead, Amnesty said quoting several local sources.
"This has turned disgust with the FAZ to bitter hatred," Amnesty quoted a witness as saying of a similar incident.
In Kisangani, at least 80 Rwandan and Burundians have been held allegedly "for their own safety" since November in detention centres run by the Zairean security service, Amnesty said.
Unconfirmed reports said they were moved to the "appalling" Osio prison, 17 km (10 miles) outside Upper Zaire's Kisangani, the rights group added.

"Amnesty International has appealed directly to the Zairean Prime Minister (Kengo Wa Dondo) to release these people immediately if they have not been charged with recognizable criminal offences," the report said.
Amnesty also protested that 14 soldiers were court martialled and sentenced to death in Kisangani in a drive to impose army discipline on January 21, arguing the death penalty was inhumane.
It said: "Amnesty International calls on the Zairean government to ensure that its forces respect the human rights of the unarmed civilians -- including the displaced and refugees."
It also called on governments to stop supplying weapons and military personnel to armed groups in the region.
